title_tag: Are Ayurvedic Herbs Safe? Heavy Metals and NPNs
meta_description: Some are, some are not. How to tell a licensed Ayurvedic herbal product from a risky one in Canada: the NPN, Health Canada warnings, what to ask.
excerpt: Some are, some are not. How to tell a licensed Ayurvedic herbal product from a risky one in Canada: the NPN, Health Canada warnings, what to ask.
body_md:
Some are, and some are not, and the difference is not the herb. It is who made the product, whether Health Canada has licensed it, and whether anyone checked what is in the bottle. Licensed Ayurvedic herbal products sold in Canada carry an eight-digit Natural Product Number (NPN) and have been reviewed for safety, quality and the claims on the label. Unlicensed products, especially ones brought from abroad or bought from a clinic's back room, are where the documented harm has come from. This article explains both halves, so that you can tell them apart in a shop or at a practitioner's desk, including mine.

## Where the "heavy metals" story comes from

The concern is real and has a specific source. Classical Ayurveda includes a branch, rasa shastra, that uses purified metals and minerals in preparations called bhasmas. Done to the letter of the tradition, the metals are processed repeatedly; done badly, or with poor manufacturing, lead, mercury and arsenic remain in the finished product at harmful levels.

Health Canada has warned about this more than once. In 2008 it reminded consumers that some unapproved Ayurvedic products contain high levels of heavy metals, citing a British Columbia Medical Journal report of a man who had been taking a product bought in India for years and was found to have very high levels of lead, mercury and arsenic. In November 2021 it warned the public about products sold by an Ayurvedic clinic in Toronto after Public Health Ontario linked a lead-poisoning case to them. When Health Canada tested products seized from that clinic, 14 of 15 samples contained high levels of arsenic, mercury or lead, and three also contained prescription drugs that were not on the label.

Two things stand out in those cases. The products were unlicensed. And they were sold by people presenting themselves as Ayurvedic practitioners. That is why "my practitioner recommended it" is not, on its own, a safety check.

## What an NPN tells you, and what it does not

Every natural health product sold in Canada needs a product licence from Health Canada before it can be marketed. When a licence is granted, the label carries an eight-digit number preceded by the letters NPN (homeopathic products use DIN-HM instead). To get that number, the company has to tell Health Canada what the medicinal ingredients are, where they come from, their strength, the non-medicinal ingredients and the intended use, and the product must be made in a site that holds a site licence, which is Health Canada's check that good manufacturing practices are followed. Health Canada says the number "assures consumers that the product has been reviewed and approved."

You can look any NPN up in the Licensed Natural Health Products Database, which lists the licence holder, ingredients, dose form, intended use and risk information. If the number on the label is not in the database, or there is no number, treat the product as unlicensed.

What the NPN does not tell you is whether the product is right for you. Licensed herbs still interact with prescription medicines, still have people who should not take them, and are still sold with marketing that outruns the evidence. The NPN is the floor, not the ceiling.

## Which Ayurvedic herbs are commonly licensed in Canada?

Many single herbs that Ayurveda uses have licensed products on Canadian shelves: ashwagandha, turmeric and curcumin, triphala, brahmi (Bacopa), tulsi (holy basil), amla, shatavari, guggul, neem and ginger among them. Health Canada publishes monographs for several of these that set out permitted claims, doses and cautions; a licensed product's label follows its monograph.

What you will not find licensed, and what this practice never recommends, are bhasmas, rasa preparations, or any metal- or mineral-based product. Nor do we recommend anything brought in a suitcase from India, however trusted the family pharmacy there. The product may be fine. Nobody in Canada has checked, and the two Health Canada warnings above are what "nobody checked" looks like.

## How to check a product in two minutes

1. **Find the NPN on the label.** Eight digits after the letters NPN. No number means no licence.
2. **Look it up** in Health Canada's Licensed Natural Health Products Database and confirm the product name and company match.
3. **Read the risk information** in the database entry: who should not take it, and what it interacts with.
4. **Tell your physician and pharmacist** what you are taking. Ashwagandha, turmeric, guggul and triphala each have known interactions or cautions; your pharmacist can check them against your prescriptions in a minute.
5. **Be suspicious of fast results.** A herbal product that works like a drug may contain one. Three of the Toronto samples did.

## What this practice does, and does not do, with herbs

In a consultation I may suggest herbs, and when I do, I name only products that carry an NPN, and I tell you which cautions apply. I do not sell products, I do not dose herbs for a diagnosed medical condition, I do not give herbal doses for children or in pregnancy, and I will tell you plainly when something you have been taking should go in the bin. If you already have a bottle with no NPN, bring it or a photo of it to your appointment and we will look it up together.

faqs.q: Is ashwagandha safe in Canada?
faqs.a: Licensed ashwagandha products carry an NPN and follow Health Canada's monograph, which sets doses and cautions. faqs.q: Are the herbs sold in Indian grocery stores in Calgary safe?

faqs.q: What are the signs of heavy-metal exposure?

title_tag: Ayurveda for Calgary Winters: A Dry-Climate Routine
meta_description: Calgary winters are cold, dry, bright and swung by chinooks. An Ayurvedic daily routine written for this exact climate: oil, warmth, food and sleep.
excerpt: Calgary winters are cold, dry, bright and swung by chinooks. An Ayurvedic daily routine written for this exact climate: oil, warmth, food and sleep.
body_md:
Calgary's winter is not the damp, grey winter most Ayurvedic winter advice was written for. It is cold, very dry, unusually sunny, and interrupted every few weeks by a chinook that can lift the temperature by twenty degrees in an afternoon. In Ayurvedic terms that is a Vata season through and through: dry, cold, light, mobile and irregular. This article sets out a daily routine for exactly this climate, with foods you can buy at Superstore or the Calgary Farmers' Market, and the two therapies that suit the season best.

## Why Calgary winters are a Vata season

A few numbers from Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1991–2020 climate normals for Calgary International Airport explain a lot. The January daily average is about −7.6 °C. Relative humidity in the afternoon sits near 55 per cent, but at those temperatures the air holds very little moisture, and once it is heated indoors it is drier still. The city receives roughly 2,400 hours of bright sunshine a year, among the most of any large Canadian city, so winter here is bright and high-altitude rather than overcast. And the chinook, the warm, dry wind off the Rockies, can raise the temperature by 20 °C or more within hours, then let it fall back.

Ayurveda describes the world in qualities. Dry, cold, light, rough, mobile and irregular are the qualities of Vata, and a Calgary winter has every one of them: dry air, cold, wind, and a temperature that will not sit still. When the season's qualities pile up in a person, the tradition expects dry skin and lips, static in the hair, cracked heels, constipation, light or broken sleep, cold hands and feet, creaking joints, and a mind that runs faster than it needs to. Chinook days add their own pattern: many Calgarians report headaches, poor sleep and restlessness when the wind arrives. Those are commonly reported experiences; whether chinooks cause headaches is a question researchers still argue about.

The Ayurvedic answer is not complicated. You counter dry with oil, cold with warmth, light with nourishing food, and irregular with routine. Here is what that looks like between November and March.

## Morning: oil before the shower

**Abhyanga at home.** Warm two or three tablespoons of sesame oil (plain, cold-pressed, from the grocery store; not toasted) by standing the bottle in a mug of hot water. Before your shower, massage it over the whole body for five to ten minutes: long strokes on the limbs, circles on the joints and belly, and a minute on the soles of the feet. Leave it on for ten minutes if you can, then shower warm, not hot. Use soap only where you need it. In a Calgary January this one habit does more for skin than any cream, because the oil is under the water rather than on top of it. Put a towel down; oil and bathroom floors do not mix.

**Nasal oil.** Dry heated air dries the nasal passages first. A drop of plain sesame oil or ghee on a clean fingertip, rubbed just inside each nostril after your shower, is the home form of Nasya and is safe for most adults. We do not perform Nasya at the clinic; this is a home habit, and if you have nosebleeds, sinus surgery or a nasal condition, ask your physician before starting.

**Warm water, then a warm breakfast.** A cup of warm water on waking. Then porridge rather than cold cereal: oats or cream of wheat cooked with a little ghee or butter, cinnamon, cardamom, stewed apple or soaked raisins. Cold smoothies and yogurt straight from the fridge are summer food here.

## Day: warmth, weight and routine

**Lunch is the main meal.** Digestion is strongest in the middle of the day. Soups, dals, stews, root vegetables, rice, well-cooked grains; warm, moist, a little oily, gently spiced with cumin, ginger, black pepper, fennel. Alberta's winter produce is on your side: potatoes, carrots, beets, squash, parsnips, onions. Salads can wait for May.

**Sip warm water through the day.** Dry air pulls water out of you without your noticing it. A thermos of warm water with a slice of fresh ginger, carried everywhere, is the cheapest piece of Ayurvedic advice there is.

**Cover the head and ears outside.** Vata enters through wind on the head. A toque is Ayurveda.

**Keep the times steady.** Wake, eat and sleep at roughly the same times, including weekends. Of all the winter advice, this is the one clients find hardest and report the most from. Irregularity is the quality the season already has in excess; your routine is what you can control.

**On chinook days,** expect to feel scattered and plan for it: a lighter schedule if you can, warm food, less caffeine, oil on the scalp or soles in the evening, and an early night. Do not treat the warm afternoon as spring; the dryness is at its worst on those days.

## Evening: wind down early

**A warm, early, light supper** by seven: soup, kitchari (rice and split mung beans cooked soft with ghee and spices), or leftover lunch. **Warm milk** before bed, if you take dairy, with a pinch of nutmeg or turmeric and a little ghee, is the tradition's sleep aid; oat milk warmed the same way works for those who do not. **Oil the soles of the feet** before sleep, and the scalp once or twice a week. **Screens off** an hour before bed; the light is Vata too. **In bed by ten**, which in a Calgary December, when it is dark by five, is easier than it sounds.

## Two therapies for the season

In the clinic, winter is when the warm-oil therapies earn their keep.

- **Abhyanga**, the full-body warm oil massage, is the professional version of the morning routine above: more oil, more warmth, an hour of it, and hands that reach your back. Many clients book it monthly from November to March. It is $120 for 60 minutes, and because our practitioner is a Registered Massage Therapist it can be receipted for extended health benefits as massage therapy.
- **Shirodhara**, the warm oil stream on the forehead, is the one to book when chinook season has taken your sleep. It is $130 for 60 minutes, or $230 for 105 minutes combined with Abhyanga.

Prices are in Canadian dollars before GST.

## Who should take care with this routine

Oil massage and warm food are safe for almost everyone. A few cautions: skip self-massage over broken skin, rashes or varicose veins, and during a fever; do not use a hot shower after oil if you have very low blood pressure and feel faint; if you have diabetes, check the soles of your feet when you oil them and tell us before any foot therapy; use ghee and whole milk in the quantities you would normally eat if you are watching cholesterol or weight, and ask your physician or dietitian if unsure; and if dry skin cracks, bleeds or does not improve, see your physician, since persistent skin changes can have medical causes.

title_tag: Is Ayurveda Covered by Insurance in Canada?
meta_description: Usually not, with one exception: massage by an RMT. What benefit plans cover, what the tax credit allows in Alberta, and how to check your own plan.
h1: Is Ayurveda Covered by Insurance in Canada?
excerpt: Usually not, with one exception: massage by an RMT. What benefit plans cover, what the tax credit allows in Alberta, and how to check your own plan.
primary_keyword: is ayurveda covered by insurance canada
body_md:
Usually not. Provincial health care does not cover Ayurveda anywhere in Canada, and most extended health plans do not list it either, because Ayurveda is not a regulated profession and insurers build their paramedical lists from regulated or association-recognised providers. There is one useful exception: massage therapy given by a Registered Massage Therapist is covered by most plans, and some Ayurvedic therapies are massage. This article explains what is and is not claimable at this practice, how the medical expense tax credit treats these services in Alberta, and the three questions to ask your insurer before you book.

## What provincial health care covers

Nothing here. Alberta Health Care covers physician and hospital services and a defined list of others. Ayurvedic consultations, Ayurvedic therapies, massage therapy and spiritual healing are all outside it, as they are in every other province.

## What extended health plans cover

Workplace and individual extended health plans include a "paramedical" section: a yearly maximum per practitioner type for services such as massage therapy, physiotherapy, chiropractic, acupuncture, naturopathy and psychology. Which types appear, and the dollar limit for each, is set by your employer's contract with the insurer, so two people in the same city can have very different coverage.

"Ayurveda" or "Ayurvedic practitioner" is not a category on the paramedical lists we have seen. Insurers draw those lists from professions that are regulated by a province or that have a recognised professional association, and Ayurveda has neither in Canada. So a consultation with me, Shirodhara, Kati Vasti and spiritual healing are, as a rule, paid out of pocket.

**Massage therapy is different.** Most plans cover massage therapy when it is performed by a Registered Massage Therapist who belongs to an association the insurer recognises. I am an RMT. When the service you receive is massage therapy, Abhyanga being the clearest example, you receive a massage-therapy receipt with my registration number, and you claim it as you would any massage.

## Which services at Ayurvedachalam can be receipted as massage?

We follow one rule: only what is massage therapy, performed by the RMT, is receipted as massage therapy.

| Service | Receipted as massage therapy? |
| --- | --- |
| Abhyanga (warm oil massage), 60 or 90 minutes | Yes |
| Shiro Abhyanga (head massage), Pada Abhyanga (foot massage) | Yes |
| Udvartana, Kizhi / Potli, Pizhichil, postnatal massage | Yes, for the massage portion of the session |
| Shirodhara on its own | No |
| Kati, Janu and Greeva Vasti on their own | No |
| Abhyanga + Shirodhara combined session | Only the Abhyanga portion |
| Ayurvedic consultations (initial, follow-up, online) | No |
| Spiritual healing, distance healing | No |
| Packages | Each massage session in the package is receipted when it is used |

Receipts show the date, the service, the time, the amount and the RMT's name and registration number. We do not describe a non-massage service as massage on a receipt, and we would ask you not to request it; insurers audit, and a false receipt puts your coverage at risk as well as our registration. Where a plan requires a physician's note for massage, that is between you and your physician; the note is for massage therapy, which is what you will receive.

Whether we can bill your insurer directly is still being set up; until it is confirmed on our pricing page, you pay at the time of your visit and submit the receipt yourself.

## The medical expense tax credit in Alberta

Canada's medical expense tax credit lets you claim eligible medical expenses on your tax return once they pass a threshold. For services, the person providing them must be an "authorized medical practitioner" in your province, and the Canada Revenue Agency publishes the list by province.

For Alberta, the CRA list includes naturopaths and acupuncturists, among others, but it does **not** list massage therapists, and it lists no Ayurvedic practitioner category. British Columbia and Ontario do list registered massage therapists. So for an Alberta resident, as the list stands today, neither Ayurvedic services nor massage therapy at this practice qualifies for the federal tax credit, even though massage may be covered by your benefits plan. If you file in another province, check the list for that province.

Health spending accounts (HSAs) are different again: they follow the CRA's eligible-expense rules, so the same Alberta limits apply, while wellness spending accounts set their own, usually broader, rules. Check with your plan administrator.

## Three questions to ask your insurer before you book

1. **"Does my plan cover massage therapy, and what is my yearly maximum?"** Also ask whether a physician's referral is needed and whether there is a per-visit cap.
2. **"Do you accept receipts from an RMT registered with [association name]?"** We will publish the association on our pricing page; have it to hand when you call.
3. **"Is there any coverage for Ayurvedic consultation or for services by an unregulated practitioner?"** Expect no, but a few wellness accounts say yes, and it is worth the one question.

Provincial health care does not cover Ayurveda anywhere in Canada, and most extended health plans do not list it either, because Ayurveda is not a regulated profession and insurers build their paramedical lists from regulated or association-recognised providers. There is one useful exception: massage therapy given by a Registered Massage Therapist is covered by most plans, and some Ayurvedic therapies are massage. This article explains what is and is not claimable at this practice, how the medical expense tax credit treats these services in Alberta, and the three questions to ask your insurer before you book.

What provincial health care covers

Nothing here. Alberta Health Care covers physician and hospital services and a defined list of others. Ayurvedic consultations, Ayurvedic therapies, massage therapy and spiritual healing are all outside it, as they are in every other province.

What extended health plans cover

Workplace and individual extended health plans include a "paramedical" section: a yearly maximum per practitioner type for services such as massage therapy, physiotherapy, chiropractic, acupuncture, naturopathy and psychology. Which types appear, and the dollar limit for each, is set by your employer's contract with the insurer, so two people in the same city can have very different coverage.

"Ayurveda" or "Ayurvedic practitioner" is not a category on the paramedical lists we have seen. Insurers draw those lists from professions that are regulated by a province or that have a recognised professional association, and Ayurveda has neither in Canada. So a consultation with me, Shirodhara, Kati Vasti and spiritual healing are, as a rule, paid out of pocket.

Massage therapy is different. Most plans cover massage therapy when it is performed by a Registered Massage Therapist who belongs to an association the insurer recognises. I am an RMT. Service Receipted as massage therapy?

Shiro Abhyanga (head massage), Pada Abhyanga (foot massage) Yes

Shirodhara on its own No
Kati, Janu and Greeva Vasti on their own No
Abhyanga + Shirodhara combined session Only the Abhyanga portion
Ayurvedic consultations (initial, follow-up, online) No
Spiritual healing, distance healing No
Packages Each massage session in the package is receipted when it is used

title_tag: Is Ayurveda Regulated in Canada? What to Know
meta_description: Ayurveda is not a regulated profession in any Canadian province. Here is what that means, what the law does cover, and how to check a practitioner.
excerpt: Ayurveda is not a regulated profession in any Canadian province. Here is what that means, what the law does cover, and how to check a practitioner.
body_md:
No. Ayurveda is legal to practise in Canada, but it is not a regulated health profession in any province or territory. That means there is no Canadian licence, no college and no public register for Ayurvedic practitioners, so the checking falls to you. This article explains what the law does and does not cover, what rules still apply to an Ayurvedic practice in Alberta, and the five things worth checking before you book with anyone, including us.

## What "regulated" means in Canada

In Canada, health professions are regulated by the provinces, not by Ottawa. A regulated profession has a law behind it, a college that keeps a register, entry standards, a complaints process and protected titles. Physicians, nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists and chiropractors are regulated everywhere. Some complementary professions are regulated in some provinces: naturopathic doctors and acupuncturists are regulated in Alberta, and Ontario regulates traditional Chinese medicine and homeopathy.

Ayurveda is on none of these lists. Alberta's register of regulated health professions names 32 professions, and Ayurveda is not among them. Ontario's list of 27 regulated professions does not include it either, even though that list runs to homeopathy and kinesiology. The same is true in every other province.

"Unregulated" is not the same as "illegal". Anyone may offer Ayurvedic consultations and therapies in Canada, as long as they stay within the laws that apply to everyone. Those laws are the real subject of this article.

## Can an Ayurvedic practitioner call themselves a doctor in Canada?

Not in connection with providing a health service, at least not in Alberta. Section 128 of Alberta's *Health Professions Act* protects the title "doctor" and the abbreviation "Dr." when used alone or with other words in connection with providing a health service. Only practitioners authorised under that Act or another law may use it. The Act does not restrict the word in academic or social settings, but a clinic sign, a website or an appointment reminder is a health-service setting.

This matters for Ayurveda in particular. In India, a graduate of a BAMS degree is registered as an Ayurvedic doctor and uses "Dr." every day. That is the correct usage there. It is not permitted here. So on this website you will see the degree spelled out, Bachelor of Ayurveda Medicine and Surgery, and the title Ayurveda Practitioner, with no "Dr." in front of my name. A practitioner in Alberta who uses "Dr." for Ayurvedic services is either unaware of the rule or ignoring it; either way, it is a fair question to ask them.

## What is a BAMS degree, and does Canada recognise it?

BAMS stands for Bachelor of Ayurveda Medicine and Surgery. It is the standard Ayurvedic qualification in India: a 5½-year university degree followed by a one-year to 1½-year rotating internship, regulated in India by the Ministry of AYUSH and its council for Indian systems of medicine. Mine is from Dr. M.G.R. Medical University in Chennai, completed in 2012, with the internship at the Government General Hospital, Chennai.

Does Canada recognise it? In two different senses, with two different answers.

- **As an academic credential, yes.** Credential services such as World Education Services (WES) assess a BAMS and report its Canadian equivalence, which is what immigration and employers use. Mine has been evaluated by WES Canada.
- **As a licence to practise medicine, no.** A BAMS does not make anyone a physician in Canada, and no province licenses Ayurvedic practitioners. I am not a medical doctor here, and nothing on this site should be read that way.

When you are comparing practitioners, the useful question is not "are they licensed?" (nobody is) but "what did they study, for how long, and can they show it?"

## What rules does an Ayurvedic practice in Alberta still have to follow?

Several, and they are the ones that protect you.

**Restricted activities.** Alberta's *Health Professions Act* reserves certain procedures for regulated professionals. Among them are inserting anything beyond the anal verge and beyond the point where the nasal passages narrow. Classical Ayurveda includes internal procedures such as Vasti (enema) and clinic-administered Nasya that fall on the wrong side of that line. An Alberta practice that offers them is offering a restricted activity. That is why the therapies on this site are external: warm-oil pooling (Kati Vasti, Janu Vasti, Greeva Vasti), Shirodhara, Abhyanga and related work, and why our Nasya page is guidance for home use, not a clinic procedure.

**Health claims.** Section 3 of Canada's *Food and Drugs Act* prohibits advertising any food, drug or device to the public as a treatment, preventative or cure for the diseases listed in Schedule A.1, a list that includes cancer, diabetes, arthritis, asthma, depression and many others. Alberta's rules on misleading advertising add to that. A practitioner who promises to "cure" or "reverse" a named disease is making a claim the law does not allow, and I would treat it as a warning sign rather than a selling point.

**Herbal products.** Every natural health product sold in Canada needs a Health Canada product licence before it can be marketed, shown by an eight-digit Natural Product Number (NPN) on the label. Companies that make, package, label or import these products also need a site licence. Health Canada has warned repeatedly about unlicensed Ayurvedic products: a 2008 advisory on heavy metals in unapproved Ayurvedic preparations, and a 2021–22 warning after products seized from a Toronto Ayurvedic clinic were found to contain high levels of lead, mercury or arsenic in 14 of 15 samples, and prescription drugs in three. This practice recommends only products with an NPN and never metal- or mineral-based preparations, however traditional they are.

**Massage therapy.** Massage therapy is regulated in British Columbia, Ontario, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Prince Edward Island. In Alberta it is not yet; the profession's associations have applied to the province, and the government was reviewing that application in January 2025. Until then, standards come from the professional associations, and insurers decide whose receipts they accept. Ayurvedic massage offered by someone who is also a Registered Massage Therapist is held to that association's standards; Ayurvedic massage offered by someone who is not is held to no standard at all.

**Privacy.** A private clinic in Alberta that collects your personal information is covered by the province's *Personal Information Protection Act*. You are entitled to know what is collected, why, and how to see it.

## How can I check an Ayurvedic practitioner before I book?

Since no register exists, do five minutes of your own checking:

1. **Ask for the degree, not the title.** A BAMS, an MD (Ayurveda) or an equivalent, from a named university, with a year. Diploma and certificate courses of a few weeks exist too; they are not the same thing, and a good practitioner will tell you which they hold.
2. **Look for "Dr." where it should not be.** If an Alberta practitioner uses it for Ayurvedic services, ask why.
3. **Read the claims.** "Supports", "traditionally used for" and "many clients find" are honest. "Cures", "reverses" and "guaranteed" are not allowed and not honest.
4. **Ask what is in the bottle.** Any product recommended to you should have an NPN. If it was brought from abroad, has no number, or is a bhasma or rasa preparation, decline it.
5. **Ask what they will not do.** A practitioner who can tell you plainly what is out of bounds here, and why, understands the system they are working in.

## Does this mean Ayurveda in Canada is unsafe?

It means the safeguards are on you and on the practitioner's own standards, not on a college. Consultations about diet, daily routine, seasonal routine, sleep and stress, and external oil therapies given by a trained person, carry low risk and are the core of what Ayurveda offers outside India. The documented harms in Canada have come from unlicensed products containing heavy metals, not from the therapies themselves. Choose the practitioner carefully, keep your physician informed about any herbs you take, and the picture is a reassuring one.

title_tag: What Is Kati Basti? Benefits, Procedure, Sessions
meta_description: Kati Basti (Kati Vasti) holds warm herbal oil on the lower back in a dough ring. What a 45-minute session involves, how many to book, who should avoid it.
excerpt: Kati Basti (Kati Vasti) holds warm herbal oil on the lower back in a dough ring. What a 45-minute session involves, how many to book, who should avoid it.
body_md:
Kati Basti is an Ayurvedic therapy in which warm herbal oil is pooled on the lower back and held there for twenty to thirty minutes inside a ring of dough. It is one of the most asked-about therapies among people with a stiff, tired or aching lower back, and one of the least understood, partly because of its name. This article explains what Kati Basti is and is not, what a session involves, what the evidence looks like, how many sessions people usually book, and who should avoid it.

## First, the name: Basti, Vasti, and what this is not

You will see the therapy written as Kati Basti and Kati Vasti; they are the same word in two transliterations. Kati means the lower back and hips. Vasti means a container, something that holds. In Kati Vasti the container is a ring of black-gram or wheat-flour dough pressed onto the skin, and what it holds is warm oil.

The same word, Vasti, is also used in classical Ayurveda for internal enema therapies. Those are a different thing entirely. This practice does not offer internal Vasti of any kind; in Alberta, procedures of that sort are restricted to regulated health professionals. Everything on this page, and on this site, is the external oil-pooling therapy. Its cousins are Janu Vasti (the knees) and Greeva Vasti (the neck), which work the same way on a different joint.

## What happens in a 45-minute session

1. **Check-in (5 minutes).** Where the discomfort sits, what makes it better or worse, how you slept. On a first visit this follows a consultation.
2. **Positioning.** You lie face down, clothed from the waist down with the lower back exposed, supported with a bolster under the ankles so the spine is comfortable.
3. **The dough ring.** A ring about the size of a saucer is shaped from fresh dough and pressed onto the lower back around the area of discomfort, sealed so it will hold oil.
4. **The oil (25 to 30 minutes).** Warm herbal oil, chosen for you and usually sesame-based, is poured into the ring until it covers the skin. As it cools it is drawn off with cotton and replaced with warm oil, so the area stays at a steady, comfortable warmth throughout.
5. **Gentle work and rest (10 minutes).** The ring and oil are removed, the oil is worked lightly into the surrounding muscles, and you rest for a few minutes before getting up slowly. Herbal steam to the area can be added as a $25 extra.

After the session the skin stays oiled; keep the back warm and covered on the way home, which in a Calgary winter matters, and avoid a cold shower or a cold draught for the rest of the day.

The session is $95 for 45 minutes. Janu Vasti and Greeva Vasti are $90. A package of five Vasti sessions, any combination, is $400. Prices are in Canadian dollars before GST.

## What do people come to Kati Basti for?

In Ayurvedic terms Kati Vasti is a warming, nourishing therapy for an area where Vata, the quality of dryness and movement, has settled: stiffness that is worst in the morning or after sitting, a back that tires rather than one that is sharply injured, and the general wear of desk work, driving and winter. That is the tradition's description, and in practice it matches who books it.

Clients commonly report that the back feels warm and loose immediately afterwards, that the stiffness on getting out of bed is less for a day or two after a session, and that the effect lasts longer with each session in a series. Many combine it with Abhyanga or with the stretches and routine we set out in a consultation.

## What does the research say?

Very little that would satisfy a sceptic, and it is better to say so. The published literature on Kati Basti consists of small studies and case reports, mostly from Indian Ayurvedic colleges, and almost always with Kati Basti given alongside herbs, diet and other therapies, so the effect of the oil-pooling alone cannot be separated out. A 2025 case report in an integrative-medicine journal describes a 66-year-old woman with two years of chronic low back pain whose disability score fell from severe to minimal over an eight-week programme that included weekly Kati Basti, herbs, dietary changes and yoga; the authors themselves note that a single case with several interventions cannot show which part helped, and call for controlled trials.

So what I can say is this: warmth applied to a sore back for half an hour is a sensible, low-risk thing that people have done in every culture, Kati Vasti is a particularly thorough and pleasant way to do it, and clients value it. What I cannot say is that it treats or cures back conditions, and I will not. Persistent back pain, pain with numbness or weakness in a leg, pain after a fall, or pain with fever or unexplained loss of weight needs your physician first.

## How many sessions should you book?

- **One session** tells you whether you like it. Almost everyone does.
- **Three to five sessions** over two to three weeks is the usual course in the tradition and the pattern my clients describe as making a difference to morning stiffness. The five-session package exists for this.
- **Maintenance** once a month through the winter is common among people who sit for work.

A consultation first is worth it if your back has been troubling you for more than a few weeks, because the routine, sleeping position and a few stretches often do as much as the therapy.

## Who should avoid Kati Basti

Kati Vasti is generally well tolerated. It is not offered, or is postponed, when:

- you are pregnant;
- you have a fever, an acute infection, or an acute injury to the back in the last 72 hours;
- you have an open wound, rash, burn or skin infection on the lower back;
- you have had spinal surgery within the last six months, or have a spinal implant, without your surgeon's agreement;
- you have numbness, tingling or weakness in a leg, or any loss of bladder or bowel control, which needs a physician the same day, not a therapy;
- you have reduced skin sensation (for example from diabetes or a nerve condition), because you may not feel if the oil is too warm; tell us and we will adjust;
- you have a known sesame or nut allergy (another base oil can be used; tell us when booking).

The session is $95 for 45 minutes. Janu Vasti and Greeva Vasti are $90. A package of five Vasti sessions, any combination, is $400. Prices are in Canadian dollars before GST.

What do people come to Kati Basti for?

In Ayurvedic terms Kati Vasti is a warming, nourishing therapy for an area where Vata, the quality of dryness and movement, has settled: stiffness that is worst in the morning or after sitting, a back that tires rather than one that is sharply injured, and the general wear of desk work, driving and winter. That is the tradition's description, and in practice it matches who books it.

Clients commonly report that the back feels warm and loose immediately afterwards, that the stiffness on getting out of bed is less for a day or two after a session, and that the effect lasts longer with each session in a series. Many combine it with Abhyanga or with the stretches and routine we set out in a consultation.

What does the research say?

Very little that would satisfy a sceptic, and it is better to say so. The published literature on Kati Basti consists of small studies and case reports, mostly from Indian Ayurvedic colleges, and almost always with Kati Basti given alongside herbs, diet and other therapies, so the effect of the oil-pooling alone cannot be separated out. A 2025 case report in an integrative-medicine journal describes a 66-year-old woman with two years of chronic low back pain whose disability score fell from severe to minimal over an eight-week programme that included weekly Kati Basti, herbs, dietary changes and yoga; the authors themselves note that a single case with several interventions cannot show which part helped, and call for controlled trials.

So what I can say is this: warmth applied to a sore back for half an hour is a sensible, low-risk thing that people have done in every culture, Kati Vasti is a particularly thorough and pleasant way to do it, and clients value it. What I cannot say is that it treats or cures back conditions, and I will not. Persistent back pain, pain with numbness or weakness in a leg, pain after a fall, or pain with fever or unexplained loss of weight needs your physician first.

How many sessions should you book?

  • One session tells you whether you like it. Almost everyone does.
  • Three to five sessions over two to three weeks is the usual course in the tradition and the pattern my clients describe as making a difference to morning stiffness. The five-session package exists for this.
  • Maintenance once a month through the winter is common among people who sit for work.

A consultation first is worth it if your back has been troubling you for more than a few weeks, because the routine, sleeping position and a few stretches often do as much as the therapy.

Who should avoid Kati Basti

Kati Vasti is generally well tolerated. It is not offered, or is postponed, when:

  • you are pregnant;
  • you have a fever, an acute infection, or an acute injury to the back in the last 72 hours;
  • you have an open wound, rash, burn or skin infection on the lower back;
  • you have had spinal surgery within the last six months, or have a spinal implant, without your surgeon's agreement;
  • you have numbness, tingling or weakness in a leg, or any loss of bladder or bowel control, which needs a physician the same day, not a therapy;
  • you have reduced skin sensation (for example from diabetes or a nerve condition), because you may not feel if the oil is too warm; tell us and we will adjust;
  • you have a known sesame or nut allergy (another base oil can be used; tell us when booking).

faqs.q: Is Kati Basti painful?
faqs.a: No. It is warm oil resting on the skin. The only sensation most people describe is heat spreading through the back and, by the end, drowsiness.

faqs.q: Kati Basti or a massage: which should I book for a sore back?
faqs.a: If the back is tired and stiff rather than injured, Kati Vasti is the more targeted choice. If the whole body is tense, Abhyanga. Many clients do both in one visit. A free call will sort it out in five minutes.

faqs.q: Can I claim Kati Basti on my health benefits?
faqs.a: Not as massage therapy. Kati Vasti is not a massage, so it is not receipted as one even though our practitioner is a Registered Massage Therapist. If it is combined with Abhyanga, only the massage portion is receipted.

faqs.q: What oil is used?
faqs.a: A sesame-based herbal oil in most cases, warmed to a comfortable temperature and tested on your wrist first. The choice of oil is made at your consultation and noted in your file.

faqs.q: Where in Calgary is this offered?
faqs.a: At our clinic, once it opens; the address will be published here. Until then, consultations are online and in-person therapies are booked as the clinic date is confirmed.

excerpt: What Shirodhara is, what people come for, what the research does and does not show, how a 60-minute session runs in Calgary, and who should wait.
body_md:
Shirodhara is the Ayurvedic therapy in which warm oil is poured in a slow, steady stream onto the forehead for twenty to forty minutes. People book it for stress, poor sleep and a busy mind, and it is the therapy most new clients ask about by name. This article explains what it is, what clients commonly report, what the research can and cannot support, how a session runs here in Calgary, and who should wait or choose something else.

## What is Shirodhara?

The name comes from Sanskrit: shiro, head, and dhara, a stream. You lie on your back on a treatment table with a small bolster under your knees and your eyes covered. A copper or clay vessel hangs above your forehead with a narrow spout. Warm oil, usually a sesame-based herbal oil chosen for you, flows from the vessel in a thin, continuous stream that moves slowly from side to side across the forehead, above the eyebrows. The vessel is refilled so the stream never stops. The room is quiet and warm, and there is no conversation once the pour begins.

In Ayurvedic terms, Shirodhara is a calming therapy for the head and the nervous system, used when Vata, the quality of movement, is high: racing thoughts, light sleep, a feeling of being wound up. That is the tradition's language, and it is useful as a description of who tends to ask for it.

## What do people come to Shirodhara for?

In my practice, three things bring most people to this table.

- **A mind that will not slow down.** Clients commonly describe the first ten minutes as the sensation of the stream, and the rest as a state between awake and asleep. Many fall asleep. Most say the quiet lasts into the evening.
- **Sleep.** People with light, broken or late sleep often book a short series. Clients commonly report sleeping more deeply on the night of the session.
- **Tension held in the head, neck and jaw.** The warmth, the stillness and the forty minutes of not doing anything are, for many, the only time in the week that these muscles let go.

Those are reports, not results I can promise, and the research below is why I word it that way.

## What does the research say?

Less than the internet suggests, and it is worth being plain about it.

The best-known small trial is from India: thirty people with insomnia were divided into three groups of ten, one receiving a herbal tablet, one receiving Shirodhara with warm milk for fifteen days, one receiving both. All three groups improved on symptom scores and sleep diaries, with the combined group improving most. There was no placebo group, the sample was tiny, and the outcome measures were subjective, so the study shows that people felt better after the course, not that Shirodhara outperforms rest in a quiet room. A Japanese research group has published small physiological studies describing lowered measures of arousal during the pour in healthy volunteers, which fits what clients describe but again involves small numbers.

So: there is a consistent picture of people relaxing and sleeping better in small, uncontrolled studies, and no large controlled trial. I offer Shirodhara as a deeply restful therapy that many clients value for stress and sleep, not as a treatment for any diagnosed condition. If you have been told you have a sleep disorder, an anxiety disorder or depression, please keep your physician's care in place; Shirodhara can sit beside it, not instead of it.

## What happens in a 60-minute session in Calgary

1. **Arrival and a short check-in (5 minutes).** How you slept, anything new, any skin sensitivity. If it is your first visit, this follows a consultation, so I already know your history.
2. **Settling (5 minutes).** You lie down clothed from the waist down and covered; the head and neck are supported, hair is tied back and protected, eyes are covered with a soft pad.
3. **The pour (30 to 35 minutes).** The oil is warmed to just above body temperature and tested on your wrist. The stream begins at the centre of the forehead and moves slowly from temple to temple. You do not need to do anything.
4. **A short head and neck massage and rest (10 minutes).** The oil is worked gently through the scalp. You rest, then sit up slowly.
5. **After.** Your hair will be oily; we provide a towel and a cap, and most clients leave the oil in until the next morning. Plan a quiet evening, drink warm water, and avoid cold wind on your head, which in a Calgary winter means a toque.

The session is $130 for 60 minutes. Combined with a full-body Abhyanga it is 105 minutes for $230. Prices are in Canadian dollars before GST.

## How often should you have Shirodhara?

In the tradition, Shirodhara is given as a course: three, five or seven sessions on consecutive or alternate days. In a Canadian working life, most of my clients choose one of two patterns.

- **A short series of three** within two weeks when something has knocked their sleep or their nerves. Our package of three is $350.
- **A single session** every few weeks as maintenance, often paired with Abhyanga.

One session is a pleasant experience. The clients who describe lasting change in their sleep are almost always the ones who did a series and changed their evening routine at the same time, which is what we work on in the consultation.

## Who should avoid Shirodhara, or wait

Shirodhara is generally well tolerated. It is not offered, or is postponed, when:

- you are in the first trimester of pregnancy, or at any stage without your physician's agreement;
- you have a fever, a cold with heavy congestion, or a recent head injury;
- you have an open wound, rash or infection on the scalp or forehead;
- you have had a recent neck or spinal surgery;
- you have a known sesame or nut allergy (we can use a different base oil; tell us when booking);
- you have been told you have very low blood pressure and feel faint when lying still for long periods;
- you have a condition for which your physician has advised against lying flat.

If you have a diagnosed neurological or psychiatric condition, tell us before booking so we can plan around your care.

faqs.q: Does Shirodhara hurt or feel strange?
faqs.a: It is warm oil, not pressure. The first minute can feel odd, like a slow drip, and then most people stop noticing the stream and drift.

faqs.q: Can I drive home afterwards?
faqs.a: Yes. You will feel relaxed rather than impaired, but give yourself ten minutes to sit up and have a glass of warm water first.

faqs.q: How do I get the oil out of my hair?
faqs.a: Apply shampoo to dry hair before wetting it, work it through, then rinse and wash a second time. Leaving the oil in overnight is traditional and good for a dry Calgary scalp.

faqs.q: Is Shirodhara covered by insurance?
faqs.a: On its own, no. It is not massage therapy, so it is not receipted as massage even though our practitioner is an RMT. If you book it combined with Abhyanga, only the massage portion is receipted.

faqs.q: Is Shirodhara the same as an Indian head massage?
faqs.a: No. Shiro Abhyanga (Indian head massage) is a hands-on oil massage of the head, neck and shoulders. Shirodhara is the poured stream, with only a short massage at the end.
